insights.headline: "Okay ma / sorry ma / yes ma" is the sentence you use to end a conversation with an elder so that what you have already decided can go ahead unchallenged.
insights.explanation: In E1 you say "Ehn, okay ma" to restructuring and then go and count the store alone; in E2 you say "sorry ma, sorry ma" to Aunty after deliberately keeping her out; in E3 you say "yes sir" twice to a father you did not tell until the printout existed; in E4 you say "yes ma" to Sister Adaeze and the next sentence is "I didn't stop". Your framing is that this is respect ("My mummy raised me", "She was completely right"); my framing is that the formula is a door-closer, not deference, and the belief underneath is that authority is to be shut politely, never argued with. Each formula is two words, and within one line a first-person verb goes the other way. Counted: four of five stories have the formula, five of five have the unilateral action (E5 has no elder addressed directly; the workshop story to your mother does the same job).

insights.headline: You believe that to be helped is to be held, so a decision only enters the family once it is already done; your own explanation (sparing five people disappointment) leaves out E2, where what you were sparing was yourself a year of being owned.

The word "hold" recurs unprompted in E2 and E5 for both money and knowledge, and disclosure is always a finished object handed over. Counted: three of five stories have a fait-accompli reveal; E1 and E4 contain no family-facing decision to disclose.

insights.headline: You are exceptional at turning an open, frightening situation into an ordered sequence you can execute with steady hands, and the sequence is what lets you act where feeling would stop you.

facts.what_happened: Speaker dates the experience to 2019, age 17-18, after JAMB, and frames it as the story of how they became a nurse.
At interviews the speaker gives a version involving always wanting to care for people, a sick grandmother, and seeing nurses.
Speaker's grandmother died; a nurse at the general hospital in Ijebu was kind to her.
Speaker wanted to study medicine.
Speaker scored 268 in JAMB; post-UTME result was middling; speaker did not get admission to medicine.
People asked whether the speaker's father knew someone at the school; a classmate whose father was a lecturer got in with a lower score.
There was no connection available to use.
Options were: change of course, wait a year and rewrite, or a private university with fees around three million a year.
Speaker's mother wanted the speaker to rewrite.
Aunty Funmi wanted the speaker to do pharmacy (speaker thinks).
Speaker's father said nothing; he had told his friends the speaker would do medicine.
Speaker was returning from aunt's shop in Ketu, standing under the shelter at Ojota, when rain started.
Heavy rain; gutter flooded; people crowded under one roof.
A woman was selling gala and La Casera with nylon over her tray, still selling and making change with wet hands.
Speaker watched her; speaker's slippers were in water.
Speaker said the word "nursing."
The rain had not stopped when this happened.
Afterwards the speaker constructed reasons for nursing.
Reason: nursing takes four to five years, not seven.
Reason: nursing allows travel.
Reason: nursing progression is documented — programme, indexing, registration with the Nursing and Midwifery Council, a licence with a number.
In first year the speaker received the handbook showing four years of courses, clinical postings, hours, and read it through.
Speaker's roommate laughed at the speaker for reading the handbook.
The same week, speaker went to a cyber cafe at Ojota and did the change of course.
Speaker paid with own money.
Speaker did not tell father.
When the admission list came out, speaker brought the printout to father; father looked and said "nursing."
Speaker said "yes sir."
Father said "that one is good, they will always need nurses."
Father was quiet, then asked "are you happy"; speaker said "yes sir."
Father never asked again.
To date the father has never raised the medicine topic.
Speaker sometimes thinks about the woman selling gala.
Speaker tells people they are a very analytical person.

candidates.headline: Counting is where her feeling goes: in all five stories the moment of most distress is met with a ruled column, and she then reports the column as proof she was not distressed.

candidates.narrator_frame: "Not how do I feel about it. Nobody can eat how you feel about it." (E1 L64-65); "That's just how my head is." (E1 L60); "I don't know why my head keeps those things. It's not useful." (E4 L61-62)

candidates.headline: The compliance formula is her licence to act alone: in four of five stories she says "yes ma / sorry ma / okay ma" to an elder and then does exactly what she had already decided.

The formula is not deference, it is the sentence that ends the conversation so the action can proceed unchallenged; the belief underneath is that authority is to be closed politely, never negotiated with. candidates.narrator_frame: "My mummy raised me." (E2 L31); "And she was right. She was completely right." (E4 L33-34)

candidates.check: E1 L15 "Ehn, okay ma" then L25 counts alone. E2 L49 "sorry ma" after L37 "I said no". E3 L46-48 "yes sir" twice after L44 "I didn't tell my daddy". E4 L35-36 "I said yes ma. I'm not even a person who thinks about myself like this, my friends will tell you I don't like all this deep-deep conversation.
Which I don't tell people because it sounds mad.

candidates.falsifier: She follows a self-revealing line with a second sentence that stays in it, or describes herself as soft, sentimental or attached without a qualifier.
candidates.would_predict: Personal Growth (obstacles and growth areas): she will leave any coaching, counselling or reflective practice within weeks, describing it as "not really me", and the exit will come right after a session in which she said something true.

candidates.headline: She measures whether someone cares by physical presence at a threshold, counted to the day; money and words do not clear the account.
candidates.explanation: E1 the only uncle who counts is the one who came, and the count notes he "didn't even come inside"; E2 the two-hour wait in the car is logged before any praise; E4 the son's failure is nineteen days of absence, while her own claim to Mama Ronke is "I was there" at ten to five. Aunty's 200,000 naira arriving after the crisis is noted as arriving after, not as arriving. The belief is that love is attendance; it explains why she chose nights ("you actually do things") and why her own words to people are formulas: she does not expect words to count for anyone, including herself.
candidates.narrator_frame: "She's a very kind woman, I'm telling you, she has carried this family." (E2 L54); "I'm just saying I know it was nineteen because I know." (E4 L17)
candidates.form_evidence: Durations of absence or waiting are the most precise units in the corpus (four months, one hour twenty, two hours, nineteen days, two months) while sums of money given are rounded ("eighty-something", "two hundred"). Precision follows presence, not cash.
candidates.check: E1 L54 Uncle Segun at the gate; L24 four months of the father's silence. E2 L11 two hours in the car. E4 L15 nineteen days; L38 "I was there". E5 L38 "nothing comes for two months". E3: no threshold count. Four of five.
candidates.counterexample: She credits Aunty, who mostly gives money, with having "carried this family". It does not defeat the claim because the credit is always fenced, and the two details she keeps sharpest about Aunty are a wait and a late transfer.

evidence.quote: he came twice, September and then just before Christmas, and the second time he brought a bag of rice and a crate of egg and he didn't even come inside, he dropped it at the gate because he was going somewhere.
Nobody came for nineteen days.

candidates.falsifier: She describes someone as having been there for her on the strength of money or a message alone, without noting whether they came.
candidates.would_predict: Relationships (friendships and community): a friend who sends a transfer when her father is ill but does not visit will find her cooler afterwards with no explanation; she will know the date of the friend's last visit and will not say it.

candidates.headline: In a crisis she sources help sideways (Kemi, whoever she can grab) and never upward from the person with the power to help most, because sideways help carries no conditions.

Peers are safe because there is no ledger with them; the one exception is enforced with a threat. Her account is that Aunty's help comes with a year of conversations; the pattern extends that to every vertical relationship in the corpus.
candidates.narrator_frame: "Because I knew what would happen — she would send the money, yes, she would absolutely send it, and then for the next one year every conversation will have that inside it." (E2 L39)
candidates.form_evidence: Kemi is the only recurring non-family name across experiences and is never described (no house, no dog, no conditions); the people with power are described in detail. Description tracks obligation.
candidates.check: E2 L41 Kemi's uncle. E4 L26 whoever I could grab; L32-36 senior's instruction accepted then bypassed. E5 L7 Kemi drove. E1: no help sought at all. E3: no help sought, "there was no somebody to know". Three of five seek help, all three sideways.
candidates.counterexample: E4 she lets Sister Adaeze take her through the last offices. It does not defeat the claim because that is instruction in a procedure, not a favour that could be called in.

Kemi knows because she drove me, and I told her if she opens her mouth I will end her.
I was turning her two-hourly with whoever I could grab.

candidates.falsifier: She describes asking a senior, a sponsor or a parent for help before exhausting peer options, and reports no cost attached.
candidates.would_predict: Work and Career (leadership and collaboration): short-staffed on a shift she will pull in a fellow student or a healthcare assistant rather than escalate to the nurse in charge, and a manager will later say they had no idea how bad the night was.

This is a value because it costs her (a senior's disapproval, her whole allowance, sleep on nights chosen because you "actually do things"). Her framing is that the hair "was disturbing me"; what that leaves out is the selectivity: she is not drawn to the patient with the loud family, she is drawn to the unheld one, which is the position she occupied in E3 ("there was no somebody to know").

candidates.form_evidence: Her most sustained active-verb sequences in the corpus (counting, plaiting, turning, swabbing, referring) all attach to a subject described as unattended or silent.
candidates.check: E1 L25, L36-41. E2 L36-44. E4 L22-36. E5 L34-41 the siblings whose fees have no source. E3: she was herself the unadvocated one. Four of five as actor.
candidates.counterexample: E3 she gave up medicine rather than fight for it. It does not defeat the claim because there was no one to fight ("no somebody to know") and the value is about supplying the missing advocate for others, not for herself.

And Sister Adaeze said to me one night, she said Temi, you're doing too much, this is not your patient alone, you have six others.
So I told them we were doing a competition.
There was no somebody to know.

candidates.would_predict: Purpose (personal mission): asked what kind of nursing she would do if money were no issue, she will name the patients nobody comes for (palliative, elderly, the unbefriended) and will find a private ward with attentive families strangely flat.

candidates.headline: She counts other people's failures in units of time and her own contributions in units of money, and neither ledger is ever presented to the person it concerns.
candidates.explanation: What others did not do is logged as duration: four months of silence, nineteen days, two hours in the car, two months with nothing coming. What she did is logged as sums and items: small chops with no fee, the whole allowance, eighty-something thousand, a phone sold, own money for the change of course. The asymmetry does something: time cannot be repaid and money can, so her side of every account is always technically clearable and theirs never is, which keeps her in permanent credit without ever having to say so. She calls both sides "how my head is".
candidates.narrator_frame: "That's just how my head is." (E1 L60); "It's not useful." (E4 L62)
candidates.form_evidence: Durations attached to others are exact to the day or minute; sums attached to her are rounded with "-something" or stated as a whole ("my whole allowance"). The rounding on her own side reads as modesty; the exactness on theirs reads as record.
candidates.check: E1 L24 four months, L47 one hour twenty vs L57 no fee collected. E2 L11 two hours, L68 three years vs L41 whole allowance, L43 eighty-something. E4 L15 nineteen days vs mouth care every night. E5 L38 two months vs L9-10 phone, eighty-something. E3: no ledger. Four of five.

candidates.falsifier: She states a naira figure for what a relative failed to give, or a duration for something she herself failed to do.

insights.headline: The compliance formula is her licence to act alone: in three of five stories she says "okay ma / sorry ma / yes ma" to an elder and then does, or has already done, exactly what she decided.
insights.explanation: E1 "Ehn, okay ma" to restructuring while she runs her own inventory; E2 "sorry ma, sorry ma" to Aunty after having deliberately excluded her; E3 "yes sir" to a father she had not told; E4 "yes ma" to Sister Adaeze followed immediately by "I didn't stop". The formula is not deference, it is the sentence that ends the conversation so the action can proceed unchallenged; the belief underneath is that authority is to be closed politely, never negotiated with. This is only visible once E4 and E5 are in, because in E1-E3 each instance reads as a child being respectful; by E4 she is a clinician being corrected by a senior and the same move is intact.
insights.narrator_frame: "My mummy raised me." (E2 L31); "And she was right. She was completely right." (E4 L33-34)
insights.form_evidence: Each formula is two words and is followed within one line by a first-person action verb in the opposite direction ("I didn't stop", "I told him after", "I said no"). The agency grammar flips the instant the elder is out of the sentence.
insights.check: E1 L15 "Ehn, okay ma" then L25 counts alone. E2 L49 "sorry ma" after L37 "I said no". E3 L46-48 "yes sir" twice after L44 "I didn't tell my daddy". E4 L35-36 "I said yes ma. I didn't stop." E5: no elder addressed directly; the equivalent is the workshop lie at L8. Four of five with formula, five of five with unilateral action.
insights.counterexample: E2: she does openly say "no" to the family's plan to call Aunty. It does not defeat the claim because the "no" is to peers and her mother in a crisis; to Aunty herself, the person with power over her, she reverts to the formula.

evidence.quote: And I was saying sorry ma, sorry ma, everything happened fast ma.
I said yes ma.
I didn't stop.
And I said yes sir.

insights.falsifier: A story in which she argues her case to an elder or senior at the time, and either wins or changes her course because of the exchange.
insights.would_predict: Work and Career (leadership and collaboration): a ward manager will describe her as respectful and easy, and will only discover months later that a protocol she agreed to was never followed on her shifts; she could check whether any supervisor has ever heard her disagree in the room.

insights.headline: She believes that to be helped is to be held, so she only lets a decision into the family once it is a fait accompli; her own explanation (sparing five people disappointment) leaves out E2, where the thing she is sparing is herself a year of ownership.
insights.explanation: E2 gives the mechanism in her own metaphor: help makes you "walk in a way that doesn't disturb their hand", and the cost of one phone call would be that "every conversation will have that inside it" for a year. E3 she brings the printout after admission; E5 she will speak "when it is already done". In E5 she connects E3 and E5 herself ("Wow. I never thought about that") but not E2, and E2 is the story that shows the secrecy is not altruism: what she is pre-empting is a claim on her, not their sadness. Compounding: only with E5 in do the three fait-accompli reveals line up as one policy.
insights.narrator_frame: "Five people are disappointed instead of one." (E5 L26); "It's not that. My mummy would be happy, honestly." (E5 L19-20)
insights.form_evidence: The verb "hold" recurs unprompted in E2 (holding you up, their hand) and E5 (a thing that everybody is holding) as the image for both money and knowledge. Disclosure is always framed as a physical transfer of an object already finished ("I brought the printout", "in my hand").
insights.check: E2 L37-44: acted, then told Aunty. E3 L44-45: acted, then told daddy with printout. E5 L17, L27-29: acting, will tell when done. Three of five; E1 and E4 have no family-facing decision to disclose.
insights.counterexample: E5 she does tell Kemi in advance. It does not defeat the claim because Kemi is a peer who holds nothing over her, and she is threatened ("I will end her") to keep the fact from reaching anyone who could.

evidence.quote: It's like, when somebody is holding you up, you start to walk in a way that doesn't disturb their hand.
Because the moment I say it, it becomes a thing that everybody is holding, and then if it doesn't work, I'm not the only one that it didn't work for.
I told him after, when the admission list came out, I brought the printout and I said Daddy, see, I got admission, and he looked at it and he said, nursing.
I never thought about that.

insights.falsifier: She describes bringing an unfinished plan to her mother, father or Aunty and asking what they think before acting.
insights.would_predict: Relationships (marriage and partnership): a future partner will first hear about a job application, a course or a move when the acceptance letter exists; if the partner names this as being shut out she will list the reasons it was kinder.

insights.headline: She is exceptional at turning an open, frightening situation into an ordered sequence she can execute with steady hands, and it lights her up; the sequence is what lets her act where feeling would stop her.
insights.explanation: E1 she ruled a book into item/quantity/days at fourteen with nobody asking; E3 the syllabus and licence number are what she "actually liked a lot" and the handbook was read "like a novel"; E4 the last offices had "an order" and inside it her hands were "completely steady"; E5 the NMC route becomes three columns and a currency sensitivity. Others already come to her for it: the younger ones bring their questions to Sister Temi, the BP crisis was routed through her referral, and she was the one turning a patient with "whoever I could grab". She calls this being analytical; what that misses is that the sequence is not analysis of a choice, it is the thing that lets her act where feeling would stop her, and she is at her best exactly there.
insights.narrator_frame: "I tell them I'm a very analytical person." (E3 L59); "when you can see the whole staircase, you can climb anything." (E3 L41)
insights.form_evidence: Energy words attach only to sequences: "liked that a lot", "like a novel", "calm, everything is steps". Nothing else in the corpus is described as liked except hearing her mother from the kitchen.
insights.check: E1 L26-33. E3 L35-41. E4 L42-46. E5 L12-16, L49. Four of five; E2 has the envelope but no sequence she built.
insights.counterexample: The decisions themselves (E3, E5) are explicitly not sequenced, they arrive at a bus stop. It does not defeat the claim because the genius is in execution once a direction exists, and both stories show the sequence built within days of the decision.

evidence.quote: When I got the handbook in first year and I saw the whole four years laid out, courses, clinical postings, hours, I read it like a novel.
And I remember while we were doing it, my hands were completely steady and my mind was completely clear, and afterwards I went to the changing room and I sat on the bench and I was fine.
I had an exercise book, one Olympic 40-leaves, and I ruled it.

insights.falsifier: She describes a procedure or protocol as tedious, or reports freezing during a stepwise emergency.
insights.would_predict: Work and Career (career direction): she will be drawn to theatre, ICU, resus or emergency nursing over general or community wards, will be the student who writes the checklist others copy, and will describe a cardiac arrest as calmer than a family meeting.

insights.headline: At fourteen she took over the household's counting from a father sitting in the dark, and E5 shows she now believes the house cannot stand if she leaves it: the role she improvised is the constraint on her own life.
insights.explanation: E1 the father sits with a dead remote while she goes to the store and rules a book, unasked; E2 when the father's BP goes she says "give me small time" and runs the crisis; E5 the reason she may not go is not homesickness but "who will count what is remaining" and who will be there for the next BP episode. The belief is that she is the load-bearing member and the other adults are weather ("sometimes something comes"). Only with E5 in does the 2016 improvisation read as a permanent post: she is weighing a UK salary against a job nobody gave her and nobody has taken back.

insights.form_evidence: Her parents appear as grammatical objects or as weather ("the television will not be on", "sometimes nothing comes"); she is the only household member with sustained active verbs across all five stories. The mother, who kept the store in E1, is never named as someone who could count.
insights.check: E1 L18-35. E2 L36-44. E5 L34-41, L50-51. Three of five; E3 and E4 are outside the household.
insights.counterexample: E5 says the mother's frozen food business "is doing okay", which credits her with agency. It does not defeat the claim because the next clause removes it ("but it's not school fees okay") and the mother is not named as a candidate for the counting.

insights.headline: The public identity is "analytical", but in five of five stories the act comes first and the analysis is built afterwards to hold it in place, and it runs on small acts (receipts, a comb, a store count) as well as the big decisions she admits it for.
insights.explanation: E1 she counted "and I don't even know why"; E2 she keeps receipts and "doesn't know why"; E3 "then after, I built all the reasons"; E4 the comb is in her bag without a plan; E5 she sat the IELTS first and only "after I got the result" opened the NMC site and made columns. The sequence is uniform: an unexplained act, then a ruled book that makes it look reasoned. What the analytical label does for her is convert a person who is moved by things she cannot name into a person who can be presented at interviews.

insights.check: E1 L25 "I don't even know why I did it". E2 L21 "I don't know why I do that". E3 L29-30 "there was no reasoning". E4 L61 "I don't know why my head keeps those things". E5 L12 columns after the test; L53 "my mouth will say it". Five of five.

insights.would_predict: Identity (learning style and preferences): on any personality or strengths assessment she will score and describe herself as a planner; two close friends asked separately will say she springs finished decisions on them.

insights.headline: "Okay ma / sorry ma / yes ma" is the sentence you use to end a conversation with an elder so that what you have already decided can go ahead unchallenged.
insights.explanation: In E1 you say "Ehn, okay ma" to restructuring and then go and count the store alone; in E2 you say "sorry ma, sorry ma" to Aunty after deliberately keeping her out; in E3 you say "yes sir" twice to a father you did not tell until the printout existed; in E4 you say "yes ma" to Sister Adaeze and the next sentence is "I didn't stop". Your framing is that this is respect ("My mummy raised me", "She was completely right"); my framing is that the formula is a door-closer, not deference, and the belief underneath is that authority is to be shut politely, never argued with. Each formula is two words, and within one line a first-person verb goes the other way. Counted: four of five stories have the formula, five of five have the unilateral action (E5 has no elder addressed directly; the workshop story to your mother does the same job).

insights.headline: You are exceptional at turning an open, frightening situation into an ordered sequence you can execute with steady hands, and the sequence is what lets you act where feeling would stop you.
insights.explanation: E1 you ruled a book into item/quantity/days at fourteen with nobody asking; E3 the syllabus and licence number are the parts you "actually liked a lot" and the handbook was read "like a novel"; E4 the last offices had "an order" and inside it your hands were "completely steady"; E5 the NMC route becomes three columns and a pound sensitivity. People already route through you for it: the younger ones bring their questions to Sister Temi, the BP crisis went through your referral, you were the one turning a patient with "whoever I could grab". You call this being analytical; what that misses is that the sequence is not analysis of a choice, it is the thing that lets you move, and every energy word in the corpus attaches to a sequence ("liked that a lot", "like a novel", "calm, everything is steps"); nothing else is described as liked except hearing your mother from the kitchen. Counted: four of five stories; E2 has the envelope but no sequence you built.
